claims.text: The initial HEA is a single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Prolonged mechanical loading at elevated temperature causes certain elements in the HEA to diffuse preferentially to grain boundaries.
Elemental segregation at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength increases susceptibility to brittle fracture.
Grain-boundary elemental segregation governs the loss of toughness and onset of brittle fracture in the HEA.
After prolonged loading at 600–800°C for 100–500 hours, the alloy will have lower toughness than its initial baseline.
After prolonged loading at 600–800°C for 100–500 hours, the alloy will show a greater tendency toward brittle fracture than its initial baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase solid-solution HEAs exposed to elevated temperature and mechanical stress for extended periods.
The identity of the segregating elements and the embrittlement rate depend on alloy composition and temperature.

Elemental segregation can be assessed by transmission electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, while toughness and fracture behavior can be assessed by impact and tensile testing.
The hypothesis is falsified if no significant grain-boundary segregation is observed or if toughness and fracture behavior remain unchanged after exposure.
